Perhaps even worse -- in some ways – is the Attorney General’s refusal to defend the state’s laws as specifically required in the state’s constitution. Bill Lockyer is certainly much better than his predecessor, Dan Lungren, but with all his good intentions he refuses to take on the politically powerful sheriffs and DAs who have put themselves above the law.
See
California Constitution Specifically Prohibits State Officials From Using Federal Laws
As An Excuse For Not Enforcing State Laws Like Prop 215 Without A Court Ruling.

and links

This article is about medical marijuana, of course, but the real subject is something that should be of concern to everyone – whatever their views on cannabis – the lawlessness of the lawmen.

What other laws will they choose not to obey?)

WHAT PART OF 'EXEMPT' DO DISTRICT ATTORNEYS STILL NOT UNDERSTAND?

By Steve Kubby, AMMA National Director
See
Orange County Board Of Supervisors Send Placer Prosecutor Tape Of Kubby Speech.
and
The Kubbys and The Prosecutor – An Insight into Pathological Prosecution
and
Steve Kubby’s Interview With A Nark
and
On 1st Anniversary Of His Arrest Steve Kubby Notes Plight Of Other Medical Marijuana Patients
The official State of California interpretation of Prop. 215 was issued to all California voters, in the 1996 California Ballot Guide. Written by Attorney General Dan Lungren, California's Title and Summary for Proposition 215 made legally binding representations to voters about what would happen if Prop. 215 was passed.

According to this official summary of Prop. 215, the State of California went on record that patients and defined caregivers are EXEMPT from criminal laws regarding marijuana. The State of California specifically told the voters that Prop. 215 would exempt:

"...patients and defined caregivers who possess or cultivate marijuana for
medical treatment recommended by a physician FROM CRIMINAL LAWS which
otherwise prohibit POSSESSION OR CULTIVATION OF MARIJUANA. " [emphasis added]
[source: http://vote96.ss.ca.gov/Vote96/html/BP/215.htm]

This official summary is quite clear, patients and caregivers are exempt from criminal laws which would OTHERWISE PROHIBIT cultivation by patients and caregivers. The term " otherwise prohibit, " clearly means you can't use legal loopholes to try to snare patients or caregivers with charges like 'too many plants' or 'intent to sell'.

California's official summary also says you can't " prohibit possession " of medical cannabis. If you can't prohibit bona fide patients from legally possessing this medicine, then logically bona fide patients have the right all the rights of possession, including the right to buy or sell or transport their legal property. The 11th word in the Compassionate Use Act is " obtain. " How can you obtain something as your legal property and not be
able to buy it or transport it?

Despite this binding statement of official policy by the State of California to its voters, many district attorneys are now waging war against sick people in California, charging bona fide patients with crimes for which they are supposed to be exempt.

That is certainly not what voters were told in the official ballot argument against Prop. 215 by James P. Fox, President of the California District Attorneys Association, who proclaimed:

" Proposition 215 will provide new legal loopholes for drug dealers to avoid arrest and prosecution . . . This initiative allows unlimited quantities of marijuana to be grown anywhere . . . in backyards or near schoolyards without any regulation or restrictions... It is marijuana legalization. "
[source:http://vote96.ss.ca.gov/Vote96/html/BP/215noarg.htm]

Gosh, if drug dealers would be able to avoid arrest and prosecution under Prop. 215, you'd think bona fide patients would be totally safe from arrest and prosecution. Think again.

Once Prop 215 passed, district attorneys immediately began looking for ways to gut the new law. Afraid to challenge this law directly and ignoring the official Prop. 215 title and summary, district attorneys began using sick people instead, who are weak and unable to defend themselves, to erode away the law and the rights granted by it.

The truth is that Prop. 215, now known as the Compassionate Use Act is a well-written law that provides everything patients and caregivers need in terms of legal rights. Only the police and prosecutors have a problem with the law. If the Compassionate Use Act is a 'bad law' as they claim, then why has it gone unchallenged in appellate court? The answer is that district attorneys know voters have every right to pass such a law.

The State of California and the District Attorneys Association have gone on record that the Compassionate Use Act exempts patients, caregivers and physicians from arrest and prosecution, yet the arrests and prosecutions continue in record numbers.

What part of " EXEMPT, " do district attorneys still not understand?
